name: Atlantic Canada: Nova Scotia and Newfoundland

cities.base: The north end, between Agricola and Gottingen above Cornwallis Street. The restaurants that matter are on those two streets, the Citadel is fifteen minutes downhill on foot, and you avoid paying water
cities.name: Halifax

cities.base: No beds worth taking. This is a half day out of Halifax on Route 333, done either before 10:00 or after 16:00, with the lobster supper at Hubbards on the far end of it.
cities.name: Peggy's Cove and St Margarets Bay

cities.base: Old Town Lunenburg, above Montague Street. Everything in town is inside eight blocks and downhill, Blue Rocks is a ten minute drive, and the rooms with a harbour view cost double for the same bed.
cities.name: Lunenburg and the South Shore

cities.base: Ingonish, on the east side of Cape Breton Highlands National Park. Three of the best trails are within fifteen minutes, the park gate is at the end of the road, and you are an hour from Baddeck for th
cities.name: Ingonish and the Cabot Trail

cities.base: The west side of the park, reached over the top from Ingonish. Beds exist in Chéticamp but you do not need them: the Skyline, the Acadian village and the Ceilidh Trail pubs south of it all fit into on
cities.name: Chéticamp and the Skyline

cities.base: Downtown, on or just above Duckworth Street between Signal Hill and the Rooms. You walk to every restaurant and every pub, and the hill means you never need the car until you leave. Halifax to St John
cities.name: St John's

cities.base: No beds. The southern shore run out of St John's: the cape at sunrise, fish and chips in Petty Harbour, and the puffin and whale boat from Bay Bulls in the afternoon.
cities.name: Cape Spear, Petty Harbour and the Bay Bulls boats

cities.base: Trinity or Port Rexton, at the neck of the peninsula. The Skerwink trailhead is five minutes away, the brewery and the coffee shop are in Port Rexton, and Bonavista and Elliston are an hour up the roa
cities.name: The Bonavista Peninsula: Trinity, Port Rexton and Bonavista

cities.base: Rocky Harbour or Norris Point, on the north arm of Bonne Bay. Western Brook Pond is 30 minutes north, the Gros Morne Mountain trailhead 10 minutes south, and the Tablelands 45 minutes around the bay.
cities.name: Gros Morne

places.name: Halifax Citadel
places.note: A star fort on the hill the town was built around, with kilted interpreters and a gun fired at noon every day. Full programs run 7 May to 5 November 2026; outside that the grounds stay open but the ramparts and exhibits shut. Adult admission is 22 Canadian dollars.

places.name: Maritime Museum of the Atlantic
places.note: The Titanic gallery gets the crowd but the Halifax Explosion room is the one that lands, because the blast happened two blocks from here and killed 1,800 people. Open daily 27 April to 31 October, closed Mondays in winter, and free Tuesdays 16:00 to 20:00.

places.name: Bar Kismet
places.note: Small, family run, and the best dinner in the city: handmade pasta, whatever came off the boat, and a wine list that knows what it is doing. Closed Mondays, and you book it before you book the flight.

places.name: EDNA
places.note: A one room bistro on Gottingen that has held its standard for a decade: a good steak, better fish, and a bar you can eat at alone without anyone making a thing of it. Supper only, seven nights from May 2026.

places.name: The Highwayman
places.note: Spanish and Portuguese small plates, sherry by the glass and vermouth on tap, at a bar built for standing. Good late when everything else downtown has turned into a sports room; confirm the day, their opening days have moved around.

places.name: Halifax Seaport Farmers' Market
places.note: Saturday 07:00 to 15:00 is the real market with the farmers in it; Sunday 09:00 to 15:00 is half of that and the weekday version is a food court with a view. Go Saturday before 10:00 for the Tanzanian coffee stall and the oat cakes.

places.name: Africville Museum
places.note: A rebuilt church on the ground where the city bulldozed a Black community in the 1960s and moved people out in dump trucks. Small, plainly told, and the most honest hour in Halifax. Hours contract off season, so call before you drive out.

places.name: Point Pleasant Park
places.note: Seventy five hectares of pine at the end of the peninsula with container ships passing close enough to read, plus a Martello tower and the shipping channel. The city leases it from the Crown for a shilling a year.

places.name: Two If By Sea
places.note: The croissant is the size of a forearm and the coffee is the best on either side of the harbour. Take the Alderney ferry across for 3 dollars, which is the cheapest harbour tour going.

places.name: Battery Park Beer Bar
places.note: Thirty odd taps of Nova Scotia beer and a fried chicken sandwich that justifies the ferry on its own. Dartmouth drinks better than Halifax and this is where it starts.

places.name: Alexander Keith's Brewery tour
places.note: Costumed actors singing at you in a cellar while you drink a mass market lager. Your money and your hour go further at Good Robot on Robie Street or at any Dartmouth taproom.

places.name: The Bicycle Thief
places.note: Competent Italian at a waterfront price, and it is where every hotel concierge sends every visitor. The same money on Agricola Street buys you a considerably better night.

places.name: Peggy's Point Lighthouse
places.note: The most photographed lighthouse in Canada, on granite scoured flat by ice. Worth one hour before 10:00 or after 16:00; between 11:00 and 15:00 it is buses and you will not get a photograph without forty people in it. The black rock closest to the water kills someone most years.

places.name: The Peggy's Cove viewing deck
places.note: A wheelchair accessible deck and ramp system built in 2021 that gets everyone onto the rock safely, and it is genuinely well made. Parking beside it fills by mid morning in July and August.

places.name: The deGarthe Memorial
places.note: Thirty two fishermen, their wives and children carved straight into a granite outcrop behind the house by a Finnish painter who lived here. Free, takes ten minutes, and most of the buses walk past it.

places.name: Swissair Flight 111 Memorial at the Whalesback
places.note: A notch cut in a stone aimed at the water where 229 people died in 1998. Quiet, unattended and two minutes off the road back to Halifax.

places.name: Polly's Cove
places.note: A 3 km loop over barrens and glacial erratics with the same granite coast and none of the buses, from an unmarked pullout on Route 333. Boggy after rain and the path braids, so keep the sea on your right.
places.neighborhood: Between Peggy's Cove and Indian Harbour

places.name: Ryer Lobsters
places.note: A pound on the wharf where the boats land, selling cooked lobster and rolls to eat at a picnic table. Seasonal and weather dependent, cash is smoother than card, and it is a fraction of what the Sou'Wester charges up the road.

places.name: The Sou'Wester
places.note: The only restaurant at the lighthouse, which is the whole of its argument. Frozen scallops, a queue of coach parties and gingerbread at the till. Eat at Ryer Lobsters or wait for Hubbards.

places.name: The Shore Club lobster supper
places.note: A 1946 dance hall doing the lobster supper properly: a whole boiled lobster, mussels, salad and strawberry shortcake at long tables, then a band and a dance floor on Saturdays. Season runs 10 May to 10 October 2026, book it, and early and late in the season not every night is served.

places.name: Queensland Beach
places.note: White sand, supervised in July and August, and the warmest swimming water on this coast, which still means about 18 degrees on a good August day. Five minutes from the Shore Club, which makes the order of the day obvious.

places.name: Bayswater Beach
places.note: Quieter than Queensland, on the back road around the Aspotogan, with a Swissair memorial at the far end of the beach. Vault toilets and no lifeguard.

places.name: Lunenburg Old Town
places.note: A 1753 British colonial grid that survived intact, painted in colours that would be illegal anywhere else, and a UNESCO site since 1995. Walk up Pelham and Townsend as well as the waterfront: the good houses are on the hill, not on the harbour.

places.name: Fisheries Museum of the Atlantic
places.note: Three floors, two ships you can board, a working dory shop and tanks of local fish, all in the old fish plant. Open daily and closing for the season on 24 October. Adult admission is 15 Canadian dollars, parking out front is 5 an hour.

places.name: Bluenose II
places.note: The schooner on the back of the dime, rebuilt in 2012 in the yard across the harbour. Deck tours are free when she is alongside and public sails cost about 60 Canadian dollars, but she spends much of the summer away at other ports, so check the sailing schedule the week you arrive rather than assumi

places.name: Ironworks Distillery
places.note: Rum, apple brandy and a bluenose black rum in an 1893 marine blacksmith's shop. The tastings are walk in, the tours are by appointment only, and the pear eau de vie is the thing worth carrying home.

places.name: South Shore Fish Shack
places.note: Haddock and chips, a lobster roll and fried clams from a small counter on the harbour, run by a fisherman's family. Lines out the door in August and it closes for the winter.

places.name: Salt Shaker Deli
places.note: Mussels, thin crust pizza and a seafood chowder that is mostly seafood, on a deck above the water. Consistently good rather than exciting, which in a tourist town in August is the higher compliment.

places.name: No. 9 Coffee Bar
places.note: Proper espresso and a morning bun on the uphill street where the town actually does its errands. Small, and the queue at 09:00 is locals.

places.name: Blue Rocks
places.note: Fishing sheds on slate ledges ten minutes east of town, still worked, with kayakers threading the islands. There is nothing to buy and nowhere to park properly, which is why it stays good. Do not block the wharves.

places.name: Mahone Bay and the three churches
places.note: Three churches in a row reflected in the harbour, which is one photograph and then a main street of good shops. Fifteen minutes from Lunenburg and worth an afternoon, not a day.

places.name: Hirtle's Beach and Gaff Point
places.note: A 1.8 km cobble and sand beach with a 6 km headland loop off the end of it through wind stunted spruce. Twenty minutes from Lunenburg, no facilities, and the surf is strong enough that swimming is a bad idea most days.

places.name: The LaHave ferry and the LaHave Bakery
places.note: A cable ferry across the LaHave River that takes four minutes and costs about 7 dollars a car, landing at a bakery in an old outfitter's store. Good bread, good soup, and it saves half an hour to Kejimkujik Seaside.

places.name: Ovens Natural Park
places.note: A privately run headland of sea caves with ladders down into Cannon Cave, where the swell booms, plus a gold rush beach you can still pan. Twenty minutes from Lunenburg, open roughly late May to early October, and the entry fee is per person.

places.name: The Middle Head Trail
places.note: A flat 4 km out and back along a spit past the Keltic Lodge with the Atlantic on both sides and a seabird colony at the tip. Easy, and the wind at the end is a different order to the wind at the car. Park entry applies.

places.name: The Franey Trail
places.note: Seven and a half kilometres and 335 metres up an old fire road to a cliff over the Clyburn valley and the coast. Three hours, exposed at the top, and brutal in July heat because there is no water on it. Go up the road and down the trail.

places.name: Broad Cove Mountain
places.note: One kilometre up and one back down, steep the whole way, and it buys you most of the Franey view for a quarter of the effort. The sunset option if you only have an hour.

places.name: Ingonish Beach
places.note: Salt water on one side of a sandbar and a warm freshwater lake on the other, which is the only way anyone swims here. Lifeguarded in July and August only; the ocean side runs about 14 degrees.

places.name: The Cape Smokey gondola
places.note: A chairlift 300 metres up the headland south of Ingonish with a boardwalk and a zipline at the top, opened in 2021. It shuts in wind and fog, which is often, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan.

places.name: Black Brook Beach
places.note: A small sand cove inside the park with a waterfall running onto the beach and a short coastal path north from the parking. Fifteen minutes from Ingonish and the water is cold enough to hurt.

places.name: The Chowder House at Neil's Harbour
places.note: Chowder, lobster rolls and fried fish at picnic tables beside a working lighthouse and a fish plant, twenty five minutes north of Ingonish. Cash friendly, seasonal from roughly June to early October, and it closes early in bad weather.

places.name: Main Street Restaurant and Bakery
places.note: Where people staying in Ingonish actually eat: oatcakes, chowder, a bacon and egg breakfast before a trail, and pies by the slab. Seasonal and the hours shrink in shoulder season, so do not count on it in late October.

places.name: Mary Ann Falls
places.note: A short walk to a waterfall with a pool people jump into, down 6 km of dirt road off the Cabot Trail. The road is rough, closed in shoulder season and not worth it in a low rental car after rain.

places.name: Alexander Graham Bell National Historic Site
places.note: Not a telephone museum. Bell spent 37 summers here building hydrofoils, kites and the first aircraft to fly in the British Empire, and the museum is mostly those. Open roughly June to October; an hour from Ingonish so pair it with the drive in or out.

places.name: The Baddeck Gathering Ceilidhs
places.note: Fiddle and piano in a parish hall at 19:30, nightly through July and August, roughly 20 Canadian dollars at the door. No bar, no amplification, and the step dancing is not for your benefit.

places.name: Lakies Head lookoff
places.note: A roadside headland ten minutes north of Ingonish that is the best shore based whale spotting on the east side in July and August. Bring binoculars and stay ten minutes longer than you want to.

places.name: The Skyline Trail
places.note: Boardwalk out to a headland 400 metres above the Gulf with the Cabot Trail switchbacking underneath, 6.5 km return or 8.2 as a loop, two to three hours. Parking reservations are required 26 June to 25 October 2026. Dogs banned, moose common, and sunset light is the whole point.

places.name: Corney Brook
places.note: A 6 km return walk up a canyon to a waterfall, flat until the last ten minutes, and it stays open when the top of the mountain is in cloud. The fallback for a Skyline day that fogs out.

places.name: The Bog Trail
places.note: A 500 metre boardwalk loop over a highland bog with pitcher plants, orchids and a genuine chance of a moose standing in it at dusk. Fifteen minutes and no effort, on the way to or from the Skyline.

places.name: The Lone Shieling
places.note: A replica Hebridean crofter's hut in a stand of 350 year old sugar maples, on an 800 metre loop off the Cabot Trail. It is a leg stretch between the two mountain climbs and the old growth is the real reason to stop.

places.name: Aucoin Bakery
places.note: An Acadian bakery on the back road doing raisin bread, meat pies and date squares out of a house. Buy the bread for the car; it is the reason to be on this side of the park in the morning.

places.name: Restaurant Le Gabriel
places.note: Seafood chowder, snow crab and Acadian rappie pie under a lighthouse shaped tower, with live music in the lounge most summer nights. Open roughly May to October and the rest of the year it is closed.

places.name: The Doryman Pub Saturday ceilidh
places.note: Saturday afternoon only, 14:00 to 18:00, a fiddler and a piano player in a pub full of people who came to dance rather than to watch. About 10 Canadian dollars at the door and it is the best two hours of music in Cape Breton outside a festival.

places.name: Les Trois Pignons
places.note: Hooked rugs, which sounds thin until you see Elizabeth LeFort's portraits worked in wool and hung in the Vatican and the White House. Seasonal, roughly mid May to late October, closed in winter.

places.name: The Red Shoe Pub
places.note: Owned by the Rankin sisters, live Cape Breton music every day it is open, and good food rather than pub food. Seasonal, roughly mid June to mid October, and it is 90 minutes south of Chéticamp so it belongs to the drive in or out, not to a Skyline day.

places.name: Glenora Distillery
places.note: North America's first single malt whisky distillery, running since 1990 beside a brook it draws water from, with tours on the hour and a piper in the courtyard. Tours are seasonal, roughly May to late October.

places.name: Signal Hill and Cabot Tower
places.note: Where Marconi took the first transatlantic wireless signal in 1901, over the narrows the whole city funnels through. The hill, the parking and the trails are free all year; only the visitor centre charges, about 10 Canadian dollars.

places.name: The North Head Trail
places.note: From Cabot Tower down a cliff ledge with a chain and several hundred steps, through the fishing houses of the Battery, and out at the bottom of Duckworth Street. Walk it downhill. It is closed or dangerous in ice and after heavy rain.

places.name: The Rooms
places.note: Provincial museum, archive and gallery in one building over the harbour. The Beothuk gallery and the Great War room, where a province lost most of a generation at Beaumont Hamel, are the reason to go. Sunday it opens at 12:00, Wednesday and Friday it runs to 21:00, adult 13.80 Canadian, and the firs

places.name: Quidi Vidi Village
places.note: A working fishing gut inside the city, with a brewery in the old fish plant and a gap in the cliffs barely wide enough for a boat. Ten minutes by car from downtown, or forty on foot over the hill.

places.name: Mallard Cottage
places.note: An 18th century Irish Newfoundland cottage doing the best cooking in the province: cod, moose, root vegetables and whatever was landed that morning. Weekend brunch is the famous meal and the one to book. Closed Monday and Tuesday, and confirm before you drive out.

places.name: Chinched
places.note: They cure everything in house, the charcuterie board is the order, and the desserts are better than the mains at most places in town. Small room, reservations effectively required, and closed at the start of the week.

places.name: Adelaide Oyster House
places.note: Oysters, tacos and a long narrow room that fills by 19:00 with no reservations taken for small groups. Put your name down, drink next door, come back. Late food when the kitchens shut elsewhere.

places.name: Ches's Fish and Chips
places.note: Cod fried in beef dripping since 1951, with dressing and gravy on the chips if you want to eat it the way Newfoundlanders do. Open late, cheap, and better than every harbourfront version of the same plate.

places.name: The Duke of Duckworth
places.note: A basement English pub down a lane, the one from Republic of Doyle, and it is still mostly regulars. Pints, fish and chips and a jukebox, and no music charge.

places.name: Quidi Vidi Brewery
places.note: The Iceberg beer is brewed with water from actual icebergs, which is both a gimmick and true. The taproom over the water is the point rather than the beer; hours move with the season so check the day you go.

places.name: Basilica of St John the Baptist
places.note: An 1855 stone basilica sited so its towers were the first thing sailors saw, with a ceiling worth the ten minute climb up from Water Street. Free, and it is quiet at any hour.

places.name: George Street
places.note: Two blocks of bars with more licences per foot than any street in North America, and the screech in ceremony where a tourist kisses a cod for a certificate. Fun once at 23:00 if you are already drunk; the music you came for is at the Ship or Bannerman, not here.

places.name: Cape Spear
places.note: The easternmost land in North America, 25 minutes from downtown, and the sun hits it before anywhere else on the continent. Grounds are free and open all year; whales pass close in July and the wind is serious even in August.

places.name: Cape Spear Lighthouse and the WWII battery
places.note: The oldest surviving lighthouse in Newfoundland, restored to 1839, plus gun emplacements and tunnels built in 1941 to defend the convoy harbour. Open 1 June to 9 October 2026, 10:00 to 18:00; the battery outside is free and open whenever the road is.

places.name: The Blackhead Path
places.note: Six and a half kilometres of East Coast Trail from Cape Spear north along the cliffs to the village of Blackhead. Unfenced edges, no shade, and it is a one way walk unless you leave a car at the far end.

places.name: Chafe's Landing
places.note: Cod caught off the wharf outside, fried properly, plus cod tongues and fishcakes if you want the local order. Twenty minutes from town in a fishing village that still fishes. Busy at 13:00 in summer.

places.name: Petty Harbour
places.note: Stages, flakes and dories in a narrow gut, one of the oldest settlements on the island and the location half the Newfoundland films use. Park by the bridge and walk both sides in half an hour.

places.name: Petty Harbour Mini Aquarium
places.note: A catch and release aquarium of local species run by students, who return everything to the harbour each autumn. Small, cheap, and genuinely good with children. Seasonal, roughly late May to early September.

places.name: O'Brien's Boat Tours
places.note: Two hours out to the Witless Bay islands for puffins and humpbacks, running since 1985, with a band playing on the way back. About 95 Canadian dollars, 40 minutes south of St John's, and it cancels in fog and swell. Season runs roughly late May to mid September.

places.name: Gatherall's Puffin and Whale Watch
places.note: The quieter of the two Bay Bulls operators, with a larger and steadier boat and less singing. Same islands, same seabirds, and the morning sailings are usually calmer water.

places.name: Witless Bay Ecological Reserve
places.note: Four islands holding over half a million Atlantic puffins and the largest Leach's storm petrel colony in the world. You cannot land, so the only access is a boat, and the birds are at the burrows June to early August only.

places.name: The La Manche suspension bridge
places.note: An hour south of town, a 2 km walk in to a footbridge over the gut of a village abandoned after a storm smashed it in 1966. The foundations are still in the grass. Good on a fogged out boat day.

places.name: The Skerwink Trail
places.note: A 5.3 km loop off the church at Trinity East past sea stacks, with several long staircases and a lot of unfenced cliff. Ninety minutes of walking. Whales feed below it in July, and wind rather than rain is what makes it unpleasant.

places.name: Trinity
places.note: A merchant town from the 1700s kept as a museum of itself, with the Lester Garland house, a cooperage and a forge, all run by the historical society on a combined ticket. Seasonal, roughly late May to early October, and outside that the village is shut and beautiful.

places.name: Rising Tide Theatre
places.note: A professional company since 1978 running a summer festival of plays and the New Founde Lande Pageant, which walks the audience around the village acting out its history. Box office closed Mondays, season is roughly June to September, and it books out.

places.name: Fort Point Lighthouse
places.note: Across the harbour from Trinity on a gravel road, with cannon emplacements from 1746 and the best view back at the village. Free, usually empty, and whales come into the harbour past it.

places.name: Two Whales Coffee Shop
places.note: Family run, espresso with Jumping Bean beans from St John's, vegetarian food and baking made on site. Five minutes from the Skerwink trailhead and the right breakfast before it. Seasonal, and hours tighten outside July and August.

places.name: Port Rexton Brewing
places.note: A brewery in a former school on the hill, open daily 12:00 to 22:00 from 1 June to 1 September and Thursday to Saturday either side of that. Food truck in the yard, music some nights, and it is where the whole peninsula ends up.

places.name: Bonavista Social Club
places.note: A wood fired bread oven, a kitchen garden, a moose burger that deserves its reputation, and a deck over the cove. Open Wednesday to Sunday 12:00 to 19:00, closed Monday and Tuesday, season ends in early October. They take reservations by phone only.

places.name: Boreal Diner
places.note: A small seasonal room in town doing cod, moose and local vegetables with more ambition than a diner name suggests. Roughly May to October, and the days it opens change through the season so call.

places.name: The Elliston puffin site
places.note: A grass headland where you stand about 15 metres from a puffin colony on the sea stack opposite, which is as close as anyone gets on land in North America. Free. Birds are there roughly mid May to mid August and gone by September. Wind and mud both serious.

places.name: The Elliston root cellars
places.note: Over 130 turf covered cellars dug into the hillsides of one small village, some still used. Free, self guided, and takes half an hour on foot before you walk out to the puffins.

places.name: Cape Bonavista Lighthouse
places.note: Red and white striped, restored to the 1870s with the original catoptric light still in the tower, on the cape where Cabot is said to have made landfall in 1497. Provincial site, open roughly mid May to early October only.

places.name: The Dungeon Provincial Park
places.note: A collapsed sea cave with two arches the swell drives through, in a field of grazing sheep and horses. Free, open all year, fifteen minutes and a very short walk from the car. Stay back from the rim, there is no fence.

places.name: Western Brook Pond
places.note: A flat 3 km boardwalk walk each way to the dock, then two hours on a landlocked fjord under 600 metre walls with waterfalls coming off them. Boats run roughly mid May to mid October, cost about 85 Canadian dollars, book days ahead in summer, and wind cancels them outright.

places.name: Gros Morne Mountain
places.note: Sixteen kilometres and 800 metres up, with a gully of loose rock you climb rather than walk. Six to eight hours, and the summit is a bare arctic plateau with the fjord lakes below. Closed 1 May and reopens 28 June every year for caribou calving. Start by 09:00 and register at the trailhead.

places.name: The Tablelands
places.note: An exposed slab of the earth's mantle, orange because it is peridotite and bare because almost nothing will grow on it. The trail is a flat 4 km return on gravel. This rock is a large part of why plate tectonics was accepted, and Parks Canada runs guided walks in July and August.

places.name: Lobster Cove Head Lighthouse
places.note: A lighthouse and keeper's house five minutes from Rocky Harbour with tide pools below and the best sunset in the park behind it. Staffed roughly June to early October; the headland and the shore path stay open and free after hours.

places.name: Green Point
places.note: Tilted layers of seabed on the beach that mark the global boundary between the Cambrian and the Ordovician, a reference point geologists come from abroad to see. It looks like a striped cliff until someone explains it, and the panels do.

places.name: Broom Point
places.note: A restored fishing premises where three brothers worked until 1975, with their gear left as it was and a guide who often knows the family. Open summer only, roughly late June to early September, and it is ten minutes from the Western Brook parking.

places.name: Java Jack's
places.note: Coffee and baking downstairs, a proper dining room upstairs, a garden out back that supplies it, and a gallery on the walls. The dependable meal in Rocky Harbour. Seasonal, and reservations matter in July and August.

places.name: Black Spruce
places.note: The best dinner in western Newfoundland, in the Neddies Harbour Inn over Bonne Bay: cod, caribou, foraged things and a short wine list. Seasonal, small, and you book it before you arrive in the park.

places.name: The Old Loft
places.note: Traditional Newfoundland food in a former fishing store on the water at Woody Point: jiggs dinner, fish cakes, pan fried cod and moose. Seasonal, roughly late May to early October, and it is the natural lunch on a Tablelands day.

places.name: Seaside Restaurant
places.note: A family run room at the end of the road in Trout River that has been serving cod and lobster since 1979, and the fish comes off boats you can see. Seasonal, roughly June to late September, and it is 25 minutes past the Tablelands.

places.name: Norris Point and the Jenniex House lookout
places.note: A 1926 house moved up the hill for the view, looking down the arms of Bonne Bay at the Tablelands on one side and the Long Range on the other. Free, open in summer, and the best fifteen minutes in the park for the effort.

places.name: The Discovery Centre at Woody Point
places.note: The geology exhibit that makes the Tablelands make sense, plus a short lookout trail behind it. Open roughly mid May to mid October only, and it is the wet weather answer on the south side of the bay.

outings.why: The granite at Peggy's is worth one hour and one hour only, and it has to be before the buses land at 11:00. Then Route 329 around the Aspotogan and a hall supper at Hubbards where they boil the lobster in the back and a band plays after. T
outings.name: Peggy's Cove early, then the lobster supper at the Shore Club
outings.season: The Shore Club runs 10 May to 10 October 2026; Peggy's Cove
outings.fallback: Polly's Cove instead of the lighthouse rocks when the fog is in, then Ryer Lobsters in Indian Harbour for a lobster roll on the wharf.

outings.why: The UNESCO grid of Old Town on foot in the morning, the Fisheries Museum for the dory shop and the aquarium tanks, then twenty minutes out to Blue Rocks where the fishing sheds sit on slate that looks like slate roof tiles. Flat, easy, and
outings.name: Lunenburg Old Town and Blue Rocks
outings.season: The museum closes for the season on 24 October; Bluenose II
outings.fallback: Mahone Bay and the three churches, plus the LaHave ferry and the bakery at the other end, all of which work in rain.

outings.why: A boardwalk headland at the top of French Mountain with the Cabot Trail switchbacking below you and whales offshore if you are lucky. Easy walking, 6.5 km out and back or 8.2 km as a loop, but from Ingonish it is a 110 minute drive over the
outings.name: The Skyline Trail
outings.season: Mid May to late October; the road over North Mountain is plo
outings.fallback: Corney Brook or the Bog Trail, both a fraction of the drive, when the top of French Mountain is in cloud.

outings.why: Ingonish up over North Mountain, the Lone Shieling, down French Mountain into Acadian Chéticamp for bread and a pub, and back. Five hours of driving with stops, on two mountain descents that are steep enough to smell your brakes. Do it cloc
outings.name: The north loop of the Cabot Trail
outings.season: Late May to late October; large parts of the trail's service
outings.fallback: Turn around at Pleasant Bay and eat at the Rusty Anchor instead of going over the top.

outings.why: Two Ingonish trails in one day. Middle Head is a flat 4 km spit out past the Keltic Lodge with water on both sides. Franey is the opposite: 7.4 km and 335 metres up an old fire road to a cliff edge over the Clyburn valley, and it hurts in t
outings.name: Middle Head and Franey
outings.season: Mid May to October; Franey is icy and unmarked in winter
outings.fallback: Middle Head alone, then Black Brook beach and the Chowder House at Neil's Harbour.

outings.name: Signal Hill and the North Head Trail
outings.season: All year; the trail is closed or lethal in ice and after hea
outings.fallback: Drive to Cabot Tower and walk the Ladies Lookout loop, then the Rooms for the Beothuk and Basque galleries.

outings.why: The easternmost point of North America is 25 minutes from downtown and the sun comes up there before anywhere else on the continent. Then fish and chips at Chafe's Landing in Petty Harbour and the 2 hour boat out of Bay Bulls to the Witless
outings.name: Cape Spear at sunrise, then the Bay Bulls boat
outings.season: Boats run late May to mid September. Puffins June to early A
outings.fallback: Skip the sunrise, do the boat at 13:00 and walk the Blackhead path from the cape in the afternoon.

outings.why: A 5.3 km loop off the church at Trinity East around sea stacks, with three sets of stairs and a lot of exposed cliff edge. Ninety minutes of walking, and whales feed off it in July. Wind on the headland is the deciding factor, not rain.
outings.name: The Skerwink Trail
outings.season: June to October; boggy and slick in spring
outings.fallback: The Fox Island trail at Champney's West, shorter and lower, or the Gun Hill climb above Trinity for twenty minutes of stairs.

outings.why: An hour up the peninsula, then puffins at arm's length from the headland at Elliston, the collapsed sea cave at the Dungeon, and the red and white lighthouse where Cabot is said to have landed. Lunch at the Bonavista Social Club on the way,
outings.name: The run to Cape Bonavista: Elliston, the Dungeon and the lighthouse
outings.season: Puffins mid May to mid August; the lighthouse and Ryan Premi
outings.fallback: Elliston and the root cellars alone, plus the Boreal Diner in Bonavista, when the fog kills the headland views.

outings.season: Boats run roughly mid May to mid October, BonTours out of No
outings.fallback: The Bonne Bay catamaran out of Norris Point, or drive the coast to Broom Point and the Arches when the boat is off.

outings.why: A 16 km loop up the back of the mountain with 800 metres of gain, and the ascent is a gully of loose rock that you climb with your hands. Six to eight hours and it is the hardest thing in this pack. Register at the trailhead and turn back a

outings.season: The mountain is closed 1 May and reopens 28 June each year f
outings.fallback: The 4 km out and back to the base of the gully at Ferry Gulch, which gets you the view up without the climb.

outings.season: Mid May to October; the road to Trout River stays open but t
outings.fallback: The Discovery Centre at Woody Point and the Lookout Trail behind it, which is under cover for half of it.

destination.name: Atlantic Canada: Nova Scotia and Newfoundland
destination.pitch: Eleven days buys you one province properly and a serious taste of the other, and the honest split is five nights in Nova Scotia, six in Newfoundland, with a plane in the middle because the two are not a drive apart.
destination.caveat: Fog is the real tax: the Nova Scotia coast and the Avalon can lose two or three days of a trip to it in July, and the Western Brook Pond boat and every whale tour cancel in it, so build in slack rather than a schedule. Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: Halifax and St John's are both small and both walkable, and between them they hold most of the eating and all of the late nights.
because.food: Lobster off the boat at a hall supper in Hubbards, cod tongues and jiggs dinner in Newfoundland, and a Halifax restaurant scene on Agricola and Gottingen that is the best eating east of Montreal.
because.nature: Gros Morne puts a landlocked fjord and an exposed slab of the earth's mantle within an hour of each other, and the Cabot Trail runs a highland plateau straight into the Gulf.
because.culture: Cape Breton fiddle in a pub on a Tuesday, Acadian French in Chéticamp, and an oral culture in Newfoundland that is still spoken rather than performed.
because.adventure: Gros Morne Mountain is a 16 km day on scree, the Long Range is real backcountry, and the Atlantic boats are cold and wet even in August.
because.relaxation: Newfoundland outports run at a speed that is hard to argue with, and a week of it resets most people.
because.exploration: Six bases, two provinces, a flight in the middle and roads where you pass four cars an hour once you leave the Trans-Canada.
